newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's ailing pension scheme needs quick action.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's ailing pension scheme needs quick action.

text.p: Turkey's state-owned social security system, supporting an army of young pensioners, is eating a hole in the country's finances that only radical reform can hope to block, experts and bankers say.

"With the present balances it is not possible for social security to keep on its feet," said Abdullah Karacik, a former adviser to the main social security institution (SSK) who has conducted a sweeping study on the issue.
"If it goes on like this it will have a debt of $10 billion by 2000 and $20 billion by 2010," Karacik told Reuters.

The International Labour Organisation, International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank have all said Turkey's present pension system -- which allows women to retire at 38 and men at 43 -- was unsustainable.
Reform of the pension system is expected to be a major issue for discussion when an IMF delegation arrives for talks on a possible stand-by agreement with Ankara in late March or April.
According to labour ministry figures, the SSK -- which covers private-sector employees -- is expected to post a deficit of 321 trillion lira ($2.7 billion) in 1997.
ROCKETING DEFICITS
The total debts of the two other smaller schemes -- Bag-Kur for the self-employed and Emekli Sandigi for civil servants -- are just below those of the SSK.

"The social security problem is extremely important -- it makes up the core of the (public sector borrowing requirement) PSBR," said a Western banker. "The government has to do something as its options are running out."
Turkey's 1996 PSBR is estimated at over 10 percent of its gross national product.

A parliamentary commission this week approved draft laws envisaging the gradual phasing in of a minimum retirement age of 50 for women and 55 for men and the raising of contributions required for health aid.
But a senior labour ministry official told Reuters the proposed reforms did not go nearly far enough and would condemn the system to debt until at least 2050.

"Turkey needs to achieve world norms -- it is no good just going to 55. You only have that rate in Uganda and I'm sure the lifespan there is less than Turkey," said the official, who declined to be identified.
"Turkey's demographic pattern is similar to that of Iran and Greece, and both have a retirement age of 65," said Karacik. "We should raise the retirement age immediately to 60 at least."
TOO MUCH, TOO SOON
The SSK has about 2.6 million pensioners, drawing monthly payments averaging 22.5 million lira ($185), but has contributions from only 4.5 million workers.
The labour ministry official said only 15 percent of those paid a full contribution: "We need to get to a level where we have four to six full-time workers paying for one pensioner."
The World Bank has called pensions "the biggest crisis of our time" as people live longer and draw out increasingly greater amounts than what they pay in.
In Turkey, as ever, added extras make things even worse.
Many people take advantage of early retirement simply to supplement the income they earn from driving taxis or businesses they then set up.

Karacik said successive governments had used the institution as a source of jobs to give to friends and supporters so that there were 20,000 surplus "other workers" in the SSK despite a chronic shortage of qualified health service staff.
LAX RULES
The labour ministry official said existing lax rules made it easy to abuse the system. "They allow someone to join the scheme one day and have a bypass operation the next," he said.
And the impoverished institutions also suffer because the state often diverts funds due to them for other expenses.
Any government trying radical change must face down unions, who slam even the present plans as "retirement in the grave".

But experts say the provision of unemployment benefit -- currently unavailable -- and the introduction of a system where "real pensioners" over 60 were rewarded with good pensions while freezing the pensions of those retiring early would ensure a fairer system, reduce the burden on the SSK and temper protests.

In a related issue, they said the government should reduce tax contributions -- higher than most of Europe -- to realistic levels to bring unregistered income into the economy and to capture an estimated four million illegal workers.
But most people fear lack of political will and a tendency to populism which has been demonstrated too often in the past.
The minimum retirement age in Turkey was 60 in the 1950s, but it fell to present levels in a populist spree in 1969.

Pro-market premier Turgut Ozal raised it again 1985 to more realistic levels but under then Prime Minister Suleyman Demirel -- who sees himself as a man of the people -- the retirement age was again lowered in 1992. Demirel is now president.
